pass1.sentence: Travellers can lower the risk of diarrhoea with careful food, drink and hand hygiene, and fluids are the main way it is managed.
pass1.note: TH factsheet: always be prepared to manage symptoms; hydration; precautions reduce but do not remove risk

pass1.sentence: Travellers' diarrhoea is loose, frequent stools that start during or soon after a trip, usually from eating or drinking something contaminated.
pass1.note: TH factsheet topic; contamination via food/water (search summary)

pass1.sentence: Careful hand hygiene and food and water precautions are the main ways to lower the risk, though they do not give full protection.
pass1.note: Fit for Travel/NaTHNaC: prevention depends on hand hygiene and food and water precautions; may occur despite them

pass1.sentence: The main aim in treatment is to replace lost fluid, and a pharmacist can suggest oral rehydration powder.
pass1.note: NHS D&V: pharmacist can suggest rehydration powder

pass1.sentence: Loperamide is available over the counter for adults and children over 12, but it is not suitable when there is blood in the stool or a high fever.
pass1.note: TH: over the counter for over 12; DV: not suitable under 12; Notts: not with blood/high fever/severe pain

pass1.sentence: Medical help is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, a high fever, signs of dehydration, or symptoms that do not improve within three days.
pass1.note: TH: seek care if no improvement within three days; immediate care for fever, blood/mucus; DH dehydration

pass1.sentence: Travellers' diarrhoea is a bout of loose, watery stools that happens during a trip or shortly after it.
pass1.note: TH factsheet subject

pass1.sentence: It usually comes from swallowing germs in contaminated food or water.
pass1.note: food and water hygiene reminder

pass1.sentence: For most people it is unpleasant but mild and settles without specific treatment.
pass1.note: Search summary: most cases mild; NHS: usually stops within 5 to 7 days

pass1.sentence: The NHS says diarrhoea in adults and children usually stops within 5 to 7 days, and any vomiting usually stops in 1 or 2 days.
pass1.note: NHS D&V: diarrhoea usually 5-7 days, vomiting 1-2 days

pass1.sentence: The NHS covers diarrhoea and vomiting together, since stomach bugs such as norovirus often cause both.
pass1.note: NHS D&V page covers vomiting and diarrhoea; norovirus page returned

pass1.sentence: TravelHealthPro advises choosing food that is fully cooked and served hot.
pass1.note: NaTHNaC: eat food fully cooked and served hot

pass1.sentence: It also advises avoiding unpeeled fresh fruit, and salads that were not washed in bottled or boiled water.
pass1.note: NaTHNaC: avoid unpeeled fresh fruit and salads not washed in bottled or boiled water

pass1.sentence: NHS 111 Wales gives similar advice, suggesting salads and uncooked produce are best skipped unless the traveller has washed and peeled them.
pass1.note: 111 Wales: avoid salads and uncooked produce unless washed and peeled yourself

pass1.sentence: Where tap water may not be safe, NHS 111 Wales recommends filtered or bottled water and advises against ice in drinks.
pass1.note: 111 Wales: filtered or bottled water where tap unsafe; avoid ice

pass1.sentence: Boiled water, hot drinks made with it, and bottled fizzy drinks with intact seals are described as generally safer choices.
pass1.note: 111 Wales summary: boiled water, hot drinks, sealed bottled fizzy drinks

pass1.sentence: Fit for Travel says prevention depends mainly on good hand hygiene along with food and water precautions.
pass1.note: Fit for Travel: prevention depends mainly upon good hand hygiene and effective food and water precautions

pass1.sentence: Washing hands with soap and water is the usual method, for example before eating.
pass1.note: plain undisputed hygiene fact

pass1.sentence: When washing facilities are not available, alcohol hand gel is described as an alternative, though it is not fully effective.
pass1.note: alcohol gel an alternative when washing facilities unavailable; not fully effective

pass1.sentence: These precautions lower the risk but do not remove it, so diarrhoea can still happen in careful travellers.
pass1.note: diarrhoea may occur even if precautions followed strictly

pass1.sentence: The NHS says the key step is to drink plenty of fluids, in small, frequent sips if feeling sick.
pass1.note: NHS D&V/dehydration: drink fluids, small sips

pass1.sentence: A pharmacist can suggest oral rehydration solution, which is a powder mixed with clean water that replaces lost salts and sugars.
pass1.note: NHS: pharmacist can suggest rehydration powder; TH: commercial product diluted in safe water

pass1.sentence: TravelHealthPro notes that the water used to make it up should be safe, such as bottled or boiled water.
pass1.note: TH: diluted into clean drinking water

pass1.sentence: The NHS says eating as soon as able is encouraged, and that fizzy drinks and fruit juice can make diarrhoea worse.
pass1.note: Search summary: avoid fizzy drinks and fruit juice; eat when able. Partly inferred from summary

pass1.sentence: The NHS adds that antibiotics do not help most stomach bugs, which are usually viral.
pass1.note: Summary: antibiotics don't help viral stomach bugs

pass1.sentence: Loperamide is an anti-diarrhoeal medicine, and the NHS says a pharmacist can suggest it.
pass1.note: NHS: pharmacist can suggest loperamide

pass1.sentence: TravelHealthPro says it is available over the counter for adults and children over 12.
pass1.note: NaTHNaC: over the counter for adults and children over 12

pass1.sentence: The NHS says it is not suitable for children under 12.
pass1.note: NHS: loperamide not suitable for under-12s

pass1.sentence: UK clinical guidance advises against it when there is blood or mucus in the stool, a high fever, or severe tummy pain.
pass1.note: Notts APC guidance, via search results; contraindicated with blood/mucus, high fever, severe abdominal pain

pass1.sentence: Antibiotics are not recommended routinely for travellers' diarrhoea, and taking them to prevent it is not advised for most travellers.
pass1.note: Notts guideline/summary: antibiotics shouldn't be routinely prescribed for prevention or empirical treatment

pass1.sentence: Standby antibiotics are considered only for people at high risk of severe illness or travelling to remote areas.
pass1.note: South & West formulary: standby antibiotics only for high risk or remote areas

pass1.sentence: TravelHealthPro says medical care should be sought if symptoms have not improved within three days.
pass1.note: NaTHNaC: seek care if symptoms do not improve within three days

pass1.sentence: It advises immediate medical care for a high fever, or for blood or mucus in the stool.
pass1.note: NaTHNaC: immediate care for fever, blood/mucus

pass1.sentence: Infants, young children, older adults and others at higher risk of dehydration are advised to seek early medical advice if they cannot keep fluids down or show signs of dehydration.
pass1.note: NaTHNaC: seek early advice if not tolerating fluids or dehydration signs

pass1.sentence: The NHS lists thirst, headache, feeling light-headed and dark, strong-smelling urine among the symptoms of dehydration.
pass1.note: NHS dehydration: thirst, headache, light-headed, dark yellow strong-smelling pee

pass1.sentence: TravelHealthPro adds great thirst, sunken eyes and dry skin as examples.
pass1.note: NaTHNaC: great thirst, sunken eyes, dry skin with reduced elasticity

pass1.sentence: The NHS says an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for signs of serious dehydration, such as unusual tiredness, dizziness that does not pass on standing, very little urine, or fast breathing or heartbeat.
pass1.note: NHS dehydration: urgent GP appointment or 111 for these signs

pass1.sentence: For signs of shock, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E, and not to drive.
pass1.note: NHS dehydration: 999 or A&E for shock; do not drive yourself
